client: I've been really struggling since I started this new job at the marketing agency about two months ago. Everyone else on my team seems to know exactly what they're doing, and I'm the only one without any real experience in marketing, so I constantly feel like I'm falling behind or doing things wrong. I'm not sure talking about it is actually going to change anything, but I figured I'd at least try.
therapist: It sounds like these first two months have been really overwhelming — feeling like you're the only one without a roadmap while everyone around you seems confident is an exhausting place to be. I also notice you came here even while part of you is doubtful this will help, and I think that took some courage. Can you tell me more about what "falling behind" looks like for you day-to-day — are there specific moments or situations where that feeling hits hardest?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, the worst moments are probably in team meetings when my manager asks for input and everyone else just jumps in with ideas and terminology I barely understand. I sit there trying to look like I'm thinking carefully, but honestly I'm just hoping she doesn't call on me directly because I'm terrified I'll say something that reveals how clueless I actually am. And then afterward I spend the rest of the day replaying whatever I did say, convinced I sounded incompetent.
therapist: That cycle you're describing — dreading being called on, then replaying everything afterward — sounds really draining, like the anxiety doesn't even get to clock out after the meeting ends. What you're experiencing has a name in CBT: it's called the "spotlight effect," where we overestimate how much others are noticing and judging our missteps, when in reality your colleagues are likely far more focused on their own contributions. I'm curious — when you replay those moments afterward, what's the harshest thing you tend to tell yourself?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: Probably something like "you don't belong there and it's only a matter of time before everyone figures that out." It's like I'm just waiting for the moment my manager pulls me aside and tells me it was a mistake to hire me. I hear what you're saying about the spotlight effect, but it's hard to believe my coworkers aren't noticing when I stumble over basic concepts they all seem to have down cold.
therapist: That thought — "I don't belong here and it's only a matter of time" — is such a painful thing to carry into every meeting, and it makes sense it's hard to just logic your way out of it. I want to gently ask: is there any evidence from these two months that *supports* the idea you belong there — even small things, like being hired in the first place, or moments where you contributed something useful? Sometimes when we're in survival mode, our minds get very good at collecting evidence against us while discarding anything that doesn't fit that story.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I mean, I guess my manager did tell me in my first week that she liked my "fresh perspective" on a campaign idea I threw out, and last week a coworker asked me to help her brainstorm something because she said I think differently than the rest of the team. But it feels really hard to hold onto those moments, like my brain just files them away as flukes or exceptions rather than actual evidence that I'm capable. I can see what you're doing with this line of questioning, and I get the logic of it, but part of me worries that I'm just going to talk myself into false confidence and then crash harder when something goes wrong.
therapist: Those two moments — your manager valuing your fresh perspective, your coworker specifically seeking *you* out — are actually really meaningful data points, and the fact that your brain immediately labels them as flukes is a classic pattern worth noticing. Your worry about "false confidence" is understandable, but there's a real difference between building confidence on actual evidence and just talking yourself into something hollow — what we're doing is the former. What do you think it would feel like to hold onto those moments with the same weight you give to the ones where you stumbled?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: Honestly, I think it would feel really unfamiliar, maybe even uncomfortable, like I'd be walking around waiting for the universe to prove me wrong. I want to believe there's a difference between evidence-based confidence and false confidence, but in practice I'm not sure I'd be able to tell them apart in the moment when anxiety kicks in. I guess part of me has been running on self-doubt for so long that it almost feels safer than letting myself believe I might actually be okay at this job.
therapist: What you just said — that self-doubt almost feels *safer* — is such an honest and important insight, and I think your voice is carrying a lot of weight right now even as you're working through it so thoughtfully. It makes a lot of sense that uncertainty would feel more familiar than hope, especially if self-doubt has been a kind of armor that protected you from disappointment for a long time. Can we explore that a little — what do you imagine you'd actually be risking if you let yourself believe, even tentatively, that you might genuinely be good at this?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think the risk is that if I actually let myself believe I'm good at this and then I mess up a big project or my manager finally sees through me, the fall would feel so much worse than if I'd never believed it in the first place. It's like I've been keeping my expectations low as a way of cushioning myself, and the idea of removing that cushion is genuinely scary. I don't know if that's something I can just decide to stop doing, even if I can see that it's holding me back.
therapist: The way you're describing this — keeping expectations low as a cushion — is actually a really understandable protective strategy, and you're right that it's not something you can just decide to switch off overnight. But I notice there's something almost urgent in how you're talking about this, like part of you is both defending that cushion and also feeling the weight of what it's costing you. What would it mean for your life at this job — and maybe beyond it — if you kept that cushion in place for another two months, or two years?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: If I'm being honest, I think I'd probably still be sitting in those meetings two years from now, heart racing, saying as little as possible and going home exhausted every night. And I'd probably have passed up opportunities to take on bigger projects or show what I can actually do, just because the risk felt too high. That's a pretty bleak picture, and I don't want that, but knowing I don't want it and actually doing something different feel like two very separate things to me right now.
therapist: You painted that future picture really clearly, and there's something significant in the fact that you *don't* want it — that's not a small thing, that's your values speaking up. The gap you're naming, between knowing and doing, is actually where most real change lives, and it's not a sign that you're stuck so much as a sign that you're standing right at the edge of something. What do you think one very small, low-stakes experiment might look like — not a leap, just a tiny step — where you let yourself take up a little more space in one of those meetings?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Maybe I could try saying one thing in the next meeting, even something small like building on someone else's idea instead of coming up with something completely original, so it feels less exposed. But I'm already thinking about how if I say something and it lands badly, I'll spend the whole evening tearing myself apart over it, which kind of defeats the purpose. I guess I'm wondering if there's a way to do this experiment without the brutal self-criticism that usually follows it.
therapist: That idea — building on someone else's thought — is actually a really wise starting point, and the fact that you're already designing it to feel less exposed tells me you know yourself well. The self-criticism piece is so important to name, and in CBT we'd call that the "second arrow" — the original discomfort of the moment is the first arrow, but the hours of self-attack afterward is the one we actually have more power over. What if part of the experiment wasn't just what you say in the meeting, but agreeing with yourself beforehand that whatever happens, you'll treat yourself the way you might treat a friend who tried something brave and imperfect?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I like the idea in theory, but I honestly don't know if I'd be able to access that kind of self-compassion in the moment when I'm already spiraling. Like, I can imagine being kind to a friend in that situation pretty easily, but when it's me, there's this voice that says I should know better or that I'm being too easy on myself. I guess I'm wondering how you actually make that switch in practice, because right now it sounds a bit like telling someone who's drowning to just decide to swim.
therapist: The drowning analogy is a really honest one, and you're right that self-compassion isn't a switch you just flip — it's more like a muscle that needs slow, deliberate practice before it's available to you in the hardest moments. That voice telling you you're "being too easy on yourself" is worth paying attention to — it sounds like it's been around for a long time and has a lot of authority over you. Where do you think that voice learned that being hard on yourself is the responsible or safe thing to do?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That's a question I wasn't expecting, and I need a second with it. I think that voice probably comes from growing up in a house where my parents had pretty high standards and mistakes were kind of treated as character flaws rather than just normal parts of learning, so I internalized that being critical of yourself meant you were serious and responsible. It's strange to think about it that way because I've always just experienced that voice as my own, not as something I picked up somewhere, and I'm not sure how I feel about looking at it that way.
therapist: What you just uncovered is really significant — that voice isn't *you*, it's something you absorbed from an environment where criticism felt like care, and that realization can feel disorienting, even a little unsettling. It makes complete sense that you'd need a moment with it, because you're essentially being asked to look at a lifelong companion and see it differently. How does it sit with you right now, even just in this moment, to consider that the harshest voice in your head might not actually be the truest one?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech
